intro: For almost all of the time people have lived on Earth, no one owned a field, obeyed a king or wrote a word. Then, in a few thousand years after the last Ice Age, that changed almost everywhere at once. People planted grain, settled in villages, built walls and temples, divided into rich and poor, and invented writing to keep track of it all. This unit follows that change from a hunting band on a ridge to the cities of Sumer, Egypt, the Indus, China, Mexico and Peru.

The evidence is not in books, because there were none. It is in stone tools, cracked bones, cave paintings, mud bricks, drains, clay tablets, carved shells and the skeletons of the people themselves. You will learn how archaeologists read that evidence, how they date it, and how they argue about what it means. Some of what you read is settled. Some of it is still being fought over, and you will be shown where.

By the end you should be able to explain why farming began and what it cost, how rivers turned villages into states, why writing was invented, and what six civilizations that never met each other had in common. You should also be able to say, with evidence, whether the road from hunting to civilization was progress, a bargain with hidden costs, or both.
bigQuestion: What did people gain and lose when they moved from hunting and gathering to farming, cities and states?

test.q: What is the main source of evidence about people who lived before writing?
choices: Physical remains such as tools, bones and sites
test.why: Prehistory has no written records, so archaeologists rely on what people left in the ground.

test.q: What does radiocarbon dating measure to estimate age?
choices: The amount of a rare form of carbon left in once-living material
The color of a stone tool
The number of layers above a find
test.why: Living things absorb a rare carbon that decays at a known rate, so the amount left gives an age.

test.q: Why did hunter-gatherer bands own little and share food widely?
choices: They moved often and hunting failed on most days
test.why: Everything had to be carried when the band moved, and sharing protected everyone from the many days a hunt failed.

test.q: How did people most likely first reach the Americas?
choices: By crossing Beringia from Siberia or following the Pacific coast
test.why: Low Ice Age seas exposed Beringia between Siberia and Alaska, and people crossed it or moved along the coast.

test.q: Which statement about the origin of farming is correct?
choices: It was invented separately in several regions with different crops
It was invented once in Egypt
It spread from China to everywhere else
It began before the Ice Age
test.why: The Fertile Crescent, China, Mexico, the Andes, New Guinea and Africa each domesticated their own plants.

test.q: What do the skeletons of many early farmers show compared with hunter-gatherers?
choices: Poorer health, worse teeth and harder work
test.why: A narrow starchy diet and heavy labor left marks on early farmers' bones and teeth.

test.q: How did a food surplus lead to social classes?
choices: Families who controlled stored grain and land grew wealthier and more powerful than others
test.why: Stored wealth could be kept, used to pay workers and passed on, so some families rose above the rest.

choices: To write poems about the gods
To keep records of goods, animals and debts for temples
test.why: The oldest tablets are accounts. Stories and laws came later, after the script could write any word.

test.q: What does Hammurabi's code reveal about Babylonian society?
choices: Punishments depended on the social rank of the people involved
All people were treated equally under the law
test.why: The same injury cost an eye, a fine or a smaller payment depending on whether the victim was noble, common or enslaved.

choices: As tombs to protect the pharaoh's body and spirit for the afterlife
As temples for the Nile god
test.why: Egyptians believed the pharaoh's survival after death kept the land in order, so his tomb had to last forever.

test.q: What made the Rosetta Stone the key to hieroglyphs?
choices: It was the oldest Egyptian carving
It was written by a pharaoh
It carried the same text in Egyptian scripts and in Greek
test.why: Scholars could read the Greek and used it to match the Egyptian signs to sounds and words.

test.q: Which was true of the Indus cities?
choices: Their kings' names are well known
They were destroyed by an invasion
They had planned streets, standard bricks and covered drains
test.why: The Indus is known for its planning and sanitation, while its rulers remain unknown and its decline was gradual.

test.q: What did Shang kings learn from oracle bones?
choices: The answers of their ancestors to questions about harvests, war and health
test.why: Kings had bones cracked with heat and read the cracks as their ancestors' answers to their questions.

test.q: What idea did the Zhou use to justify overthrowing the Shang?
test.why: The Zhou said Heaven had taken its mandate from the wicked Shang and given it to them.

test.q: What do the Olmec and Norte Chico show about early civilizations?
choices: That all civilizations began in river valleys with grain
That people in the Americas built complex societies on their own, without contact with Asia or Africa
That civilization spread from Egypt to Mexico
test.why: The Olmec and Norte Chico rose independently, showing civilization was invented several times in different ways.

write.prompt: Was the shift from hunting and gathering to farming and cities a good deal for the people who lived through it? Make a claim, support it with at least three pieces of evidence from this unit, and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: a good deal, a bad deal, or good for societies but bad for individuals.
Use specific evidence: skeleton studies, the graves at early villages, Hammurabi's laws, the strike at Deir el-Medina, the drains of the Indus, the walls of Uruk.
Explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it does.
Take the other side seriously: name the strongest argument against your claim and answer it.
Remember whose evidence you are using. Scribes and kings left most of the words; farmers left mostly bones.
